This manuscript presents BERTPhylo, a pretrained DNA language model coupled to a pragmatic pipeline for accelerating phylogenetic updates: it (i) assigns a new sequence to a taxonomic unit via joint novelty detection and hierarchical classification and (ii) uses attention-derived “high-attention regions” to restrict alignment and inference to the relevant subtree (Fig. 1a–b). On the PlantSeqs dataset (157,742 sequences from nine markers), BERTPhylo improves over DNABERT and BERTax for both novelty detection (Fig. 4a–b) and hierarchical taxonomic classification (Table 1; Supplementary Tables S1–S2), and, when combined with MMseqs2, yields further gains. The attention maps appear biologically meaningful—often co-localizing with regions of higher heterozygosity and FST (Fig. 7g; Supplementary Fig. S7)—and high-attention regions produce subtrees with better resolution than low-attention regions in multiple orders (Fig. 6; Supplementary Fig. S6). Code and weights are available (Availability).

Strengths
1. Clear conceptual advance: reframing phylogenetic “tree updates” as a placement-plus-subtree reconstruction task guided by a genomic LLM, reducing both sequence number and length before classical alignment/inference (Fig. 1a).  
2. Novel, rank-specific OOD detection tightly integrated with hierarchical classification to determine the “lowest known rank” for placement (Section 2.2; Fig. 4a–b).  
3. Attention-informed region selection is compelling and empirically supported by correlations with population-genetic diversity metrics across markers (Fig. 7e,g; Supplementary Fig. S7).  
4. Systematic benchmarking versus both deep learning and well-established traditional tools (Table 1; Supplementary Tables S1–S2), including a useful ensemble (MMseqs2 + BERTPhylo).  
5. A large curated dataset with ID/OOD structure across ranks (Section 4.2; Fig. 8a–c; Table 2), and open-source implementation with pretrained weights (Availability).

Major points that need attention before this work can be considered fully convincing at scale
1. Phylogenetic accuracy is not quantified rigorously. The central claim is that “high-attention regions” retain sufficient signal to replace full-length loci for subtree inference (Section 2.3; Fig. 6), yet evidence rests largely on visual examples. Please report standard tree-comparison metrics (e.g., normalized Robinson–Foulds distances, quartet concordance) between (i) full-length trees and (ii) trees from high-attention, low-attention, and randomly sampled regions matched in length. Include bootstrap or SH-like support distributions for all conditions to assess “resolution,” not just topology. Supplementary Fig. S6 should be complemented by these quantitative summaries across all 11 orders.
2. End-to-end efficiency lacks comprehensive benchmarking. You provide one illustrative case (“4 minutes… 0.33% of the time required by the standard pipelines,” Section 2.1; Fig. 3), but the total overhead to compute BERT embeddings and attention for all subtree sequences is not reported. Provide wall-clock benchmarks (with hardware specs) for: attention extraction, novelty detection/classification, alignment, and tree inference across a representative range of subtree sizes and marker sets, and compare against full pipelines. Memory usage would also be informative. The theoretical complexity reduction O(NL log L) + O(N^2) → O(n l log l) + O(n^2) (Section 2.1) should be grounded in empirical timing across datasets.
3. The algorithmic details for determining the target subtree from novelty detection plus classification need to be made explicit and reproducible. Section 2.1 and Materials and Methods (Section 4.1) describe a rule using “the maximum classification probability at the lowest rank among the ranks with a lower novelty detection score,” but thresholds and calibration are unspecified. Softmax confidence is known to be miscalibrated; please describe how thresholds are chosen (validation-based?), whether temperature scaling or other calibration is applied, and provide per-rank operating points with precision/recall for ID vs OOD decisions.
4. The ensemble “MMseqs2 + BERTPhylo” shows strong performance (Table 1; Supplementary Tables S1–S2), but the fusion rule is not documented. Specify exactly how predictions are combined (e.g., priority by alignment score threshold, fallback by OOD flag, weighted voting). Report ablations varying ensemble rules and thresholds.
5. Parameterization and robustness of the attention-based region selector are under-specified. The procedure divides sequences into three equal regions, scores windows of 50 nt above the per-sequence mean attention, and uses a “minority-majority voting” scheme across sequences to select one region (Section 4.1). Please justify the choice of three regions and 50 nt windows, and include sensitivity analyses varying: number of regions, window size, attention thresholding (mean vs percentile), and whether multiple non-contiguous high-attention windows are concatenated. Clarify whether regions are selected per marker, per gene, or across concatenated markers; the current description (Sections 2.1, 4.1) can be read both ways.
6. Phylogenetic inference settings are incomplete. For MAFFT and RAxML runs (Section 2.1), specify alignment parameters, partitioning scheme across markers/regions, substitution models, rate heterogeneity, and number of bootstrap replicates. Provide alignment files, partitions, and tree files as supplementary data to satisfy reproducibility.
7. Dataset construction and potential biases require clarification. Section 4.2 states that sequences longer than 1,530 bp were filtered out “to fit the input length limit,” which likely removes many full-length 28S rRNA and other loci. Please quantify how many sequences per marker were excluded and analyze whether this length-based filtering biases marker composition and downstream results (e.g., Table S3–S4). Also clarify how sequences from the same species across multiple markers were handled to prevent leakage (e.g., are different markers from the same genus appearing in both training and test for OOD-at-genus experiments?). Provide accession lists and the exact train/val/test splits (Supplementary Dataset).
8. Claims on conceptual primacy should be tempered or better contextualized. The assertion of providing “the first evidence that phylogenetic trees can be constructed by automatically selecting the most informative regions… without manual selection of molecular markers” (Abstract; Section 2.1) overlooks prior automated marker/region-selection and subsampling strategies based on phylogenetic informativeness and sliding-window analyses. Please either moderate the wording or situate BERTPhylo with citations that distinguish your attention-based, LLM-driven selection from earlier automated criteria.
9. Statistical reporting could be strengthened. For classification and OOD detection (Table 1; Fig. 4–5; Supplementary Tables S1–S2), provide confidence intervals over multiple random seeds/splits. Confusion matrices (Supplementary Fig. S1) are helpful, but per-class precision/recall for difficult classes (e.g., Rubiaceae, Cucurbitales; Section 2.2) and calibration curves would add depth.

Additional suggestions to improve rigor and clarity
1. Include ablations on the choice of using only “the first 10 layers” of DNABERT (Section 4.3) and the two-step training strategy (Fig. 1c). Report performance when fine-tuning all 12 layers vs 10, and when skipping the linear-probe pretraining.  
2. Explore stronger OOD baselines beyond 1 − max softmax probability (Section 4.3), such as energy-based scores, ODIN, or Mahalanobis distance in the embedding space, and compare AUROC/AUPR (Fig. 4a).  
3. Discuss gene-tree/species-tree discordance when mixing plastid and nuclear regions; attention-guided selection may emphasize loci with idiosyncratic histories. A short analysis comparing discordance rates between high-attention and full-length concatenations would be informative.  
4. Provide hardware and software environment details (GPUs/CPUs, versions of MAFFT/RAxML and parameters), random seeds, and commit hashes for reproducibility.  
5. Clean up formatting/typos that currently hinder clarity, e.g., “Efffcient,” “Classi«cation,” “nulcear,” “chlroplast,” numbers with stray spaces/commas (Table 2 “3,00 6,00 1,800 5,000”), and missing numerals in “randomly sampled 1 , sequences” (Fig. 7f; Section 4.5). Clarify counts in Section 4.2 (“19,887 species form 150 genera”; Table 2).

Overall, this study offers a creative and potentially impactful synthesis of genomic LLMs with classical phylogenetic pipelines. The hierarchical OOD+classification framework (Section 2.2) and attention-guided subsampling (Sections 2.3, 4.1) are promising. Addressing the points above—especially quantitative phylogenetic validation against full-length baselines and comprehensive runtime benchmarking including model overhead—would substantially strengthen the paper’s claims about both accuracy and efficiency. The code availability and extensive supplementary benchmarking are strong foundations to build on; a tightened Methods and expanded validation would make this a valuable contribution to computational phylogenetics.

Expertise: computational genomics, sequence representation learning, phylogenetic inference, and benchmarking of ML models for biological sequence analysis. I did not verify the repository code.

[Standards for images]
Digital images submitted with a manuscript for review should be minimally processed.  A certain degree of image processing is acceptable for publication (and for some experiments, fields and techniques is unavoidable), but the final image must correctly represent the original data and conform to community standards. Editors may request the unprocessed data files to help in manuscript evaluation during the peer review process; if these data are unavailable upon request, we may need to halt the peer review process until the issues are satisfactorily resolved. Lack of availability of unprocessed data can make resolution of post-publication issues challenging.  We recommend retaining unprocessed data and metadata files after publication, ideally archiving data in perpetuity.  

All life science papers published in Nature Portfolio journals require submission of unprocessed original images of gels and western blots to be submitted with the final accepted version. These unprocessed images are published in the Supplementary Information.

Please list all image acquisition tools and image processing software packages used and document key image-gathering settings and processing manipulations in the Methods.

Principles of scholarly freedom and scholarly responsibility

There should be a discernible reason why the work deserves the visibility of publication in a Nature Portfolio journal rather than the best of the specialist journals.

All submitted manuscripts are read by the editorial staff. To save time for authors and peer-reviewers, only those papers that seem most likely to meet our editorial criteria are sent for formal review. Those papers judged by the editors to be of insufficient general interest or otherwise inappropriate are rejected promptly without external review (although these decisions may be based on informal advice from specialists in the field).
Manuscripts judged to be of potential interest to our readership are sent for formal review, typically to two or three reviewers, but sometimes more if special advice is needed (for example on statistics or a particular technique). - Invite the authors to revise their manuscript to address specific concerns before a final decision is reached
- Reject, but indicate to the authors that further work might justify a resubmission
- Reject outright, typically on grounds of specialist interest, lack of novelty, insufficient conceptual advance or major technical and/or interpretational problems

- Validity: Does the manuscript have flaws which should prohibit its publication? If so, please provide details.

- Conclusions: Do you find that the conclusions and data interpretation are robust, valid and reliable?
- Suggested improvements: Please list additional experiments or data that could help strengthening the work in a revision.
- References: Does this manuscript reference previous literature appropriately? If not, what references should be included or excluded?
- Clarity and context: Is the abstract clear, accessible? Are abstract, introduction and conclusions appropriate?

Springer Nature is committed to diversity, equity and inclusion; please raise any concerns that may in your view have an impact on this commitment.
Please indicate any particular part of the manuscript, data, or analyses that you feel is outside the scope of your expertise, or that you were unable to assess fully.

- what the classification terms are;

In reality, there is a spectrum of gender identities and expressions defining how individuals identify themselves and express their gender

# Abstract
Understanding the phylogenetic relationships among species is crucial for com19 prehending major evolutionary transitions, serving as the foundation for many 20 biological studies. Despite the ever-growing volume of sequence data providing a 21 significant opportunity for biological research, constructing reliable phylogenetic 22 trees effectively becomes more challenging for current analytical methods. In this 23 study, we introduce a novel solution to accelerate phylogeny inference using a 24 pretrained DNA language model. Our approach identifies the taxonomic unit of 25 a newly collected sequence using existing taxonomic classification systems and 26 updates the corresponding subtree, akin to surgical corrections on a given phy27 logenetic tree. Specifically, we leverage a pretrained BERT network to obtain 28 high-dimensional sequence representations, which are used not only to deter29 mine the subtree to be updated but also identify potentially valuable regions for 30 subtree construction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, named 31

3

BERTPhylo, through experiments on our established PlantSeqs dataset, focusing 32 on Embryophyta. Our findings provide the first evidence that phylogenetic trees 33 can be constructed by automatically selecting the most informative regions of 34 sequences, without manual selection of molecular markers. This discovery offers 35 a robust guide for further research into the functional aspects of different regions 36 of DNA sequences, enriching our understanding of biology. 37

# 1 Introduction 40
- Phylogenetic trees serve as fundamental pillars in biological research, elucidating evo41 lutionary relationships among organisms and offering profound insights into their 42 shared history [1-3]. In addition, they play a pivotal role, for instance, in pinpoint43 ing distinct species communities to refine conservation strategies [4-6], in deciphering 44 virus origins [7-9], or even in elucidating cancer progression and guiding therapies [1045 13]. For nearly two decades, molecular phylogenies have primarily relied on data from 46 a few genes obtained through PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing. However, 47 advancements in sequencing technologies have resulted in large-scale datasets contain48 ing orders of magnitude more genes, posing challenges to accurately reconstructing the 49 tree of life [14, 15]. On the one hand, the exponential growth in the quantity of genetic 50 data intensifies computational and storage burdens, leading to substantial time con51 straints and a super-exponential rise in the demand for computational and storage 52 resources. On the other hand, the longer sequences (up to entire genomes) may not 53 only challenge the ability of computational resources but also contain inconsistencies 54 or noise, leading to misleading or less precise results [16, 17]. 55 Traditional phylogenetic tree construction methods are typically divided into two 56 categories: distance-based and character-based. In the context of species tree infer57 ence, distance methods involve calculating genetic distances between species pairs 58 and using resulting matrices to build trees. Character-based methods compare all 59 DNA sequences in an alignment simultaneously, considering one site at a time to cal60 culate scores for each tree. These methods include maximum parsimony, maximum 61 likelihood, and Bayesian inference [18]. However, identifying the tree with the highest 62 score requires comparing all possible trees, which is computationally infeasible due to 63 the NP-hard nature of tree construction [19, 20]. To mitigate computational burdens, 64 various heuristic tree search methods focusing on accelerating and parallelizing cal65 culations have been developed, such as DupTree [21], FastTree [22], PhyloBayes MPI 66 [23], ExaBayes [24], and RAxML-NG [25]. These heuristic tree search methods are 67 not guaranteed to find the best tree, but make it feasible to analyse large data sets 68 [18]. Nonetheless, there is considerable room for improving computational efficiency 69 while maintaining accuracy, making the balance between the two a challenging and 70 pressing issue. 71

Recent advances in deep learning offer promising opportunities for phylogenetic 72 inference, which can be broadly categorized into classification-based and distance73 based methods. Classification-based methods treat phylogenetic inference as a classi74 fication problem, aiming to train neural networks to predict the topology of sequences 75 [26, 27]. Distance-based methods utilize neural networks to improve distance repre76 sentation, addressing challenges such as phylogenetic placement problems and data 77 imputation problems in incomplete distance matrices [28-30]. However, applying deep 78 learning to phylogenetic inference is still in its infancy [31]. Classification-based meth79 ods struggle with scalability and cannot infer branch lengths. Moreover, training deep 80 learning models requires large datasets, but benchmark data with known 'true' phy81 logenies are rare. As a result, almost all studies use simulated data for training, which 82 may not accurately reflect the complexity and diversity of real biological systems, lim83 iting the generalization performance of models on empirical data [32]. Additionally, 84 existing applications are predominantly based on convolutional neural network (CNN) 85 structures, which may not always outperform traditional tree construction methods 86 [33]. As large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language under87 standing, their application to genome modeling problems has also increased [34-38]. 88 Due to the similarities between DNA sequences and natural languages, genomic LLMs 89 built on the Transformer architecture [39] with self-attention mechanism can skillfully 90 model genomic information by capturing long-range dependencies. Such models have 91 recently achieved unprecedented success across various downstream tasks, as exem92 plified by the generation of DNA sequences [36], or the prediction of promoters [34], 93 enhancers [40], and chromatin profiles [38]. Despite these advances, gaps remain in 94 applying LLMs to phylogenetic inference. 95

Amid these challenges, we here introduce a novel program called BERTPhylo, 96 designed to accelerate phylogenetic inference by using a pretrained DNA language 97 model [34], which is constructed and trained following the Bidirectional Encoder 98 Representations from Transformers (BERT) [41] to capture global and transferrable 99 understanding of DNA sequences based on up and downstream nucleotide contexts. 100 As depicted in Figure 1a, BERTPhylo built upon existing taxonomic classification 101 systems to identify the taxonomic unit of a given sequence without performing any 102 operations on it. The network's attention weight on the sequence can also identify 103 potentially valuable genetic regions (hereafter referred to as high-attention regions) 104 that contain adequate informative sites for robust phylogenetic tree construction. We, 105 therefore, propose a novel pipeline based on BERTPhylo, which constructs subtrees 106 for the clades of the new sequences' taxonomic units using only high-attention regions, 107 instead of constructing a complete phylogenetic tree using full-length sequences. In 108 contrast to standard pipelines that align and analyze all sequences simultaneously (e.g. 109 BuddySuite [42], ETE3 [43], and MEGA [44]), our pipeline reduces the number and 110 length of input sequences for subsequent alignment and tree analyses, thereby signif111 icantly decreasing the tree construction time. Importantly, BERTPhylo achieves this 112 speedup without compromising topology accuracy by integrating deep learning with 113 traditional tree construction tools. To validate this innovative approach, we created 114 a dataset called PlantSeqs, which contains 157 , 742 DNA sequences of Embryophyta. 115

These sequences were downloaded from the National Center for Biotechnology Infor116 mation (NCBI) and covered nine commonly used molecular markers (see Materials 117 and Methods for details). In addition to evaluating the effectiveness of the model, we 118 cross-referenced the results with previous studies, demonstrating the efficiency and 119 precision of BERTPhylo. 120
# 2 Results 121

# 2.1 BERTPhylo demonstrates the ability to rapidly update phylogenetic trees
To illustrate the process of updating a phylogenetic tree using BERTPhylo results, 124 Figure 2 presents a simplified example. The original tree comprises 677 species of 125 20 orders from Embryophyta. The sequences of these species were selected from the 126 PlantSeqs dataset. We concatenated all molecular markers of each species for tree 127 construction, with the total lengths ranging from 2 , 493 bp to 7 , 705 bp. When a new 128 species is added, BERTPhylo classifies its sequence and assigns it to an established 129 taxonomic unit. It also identifies high-attention regions for all sequences of the clade, 130 which contain sufficient genetic information crucial for the subtree construction (see 131 subsequent sections). We then utilized MAFFT [45] and RAxML [25] to perform 132 alignment and subtree inference with only high-attention regions (Fig. 1a). 133

The target taxonomic unit for the new sequence is jointly determined by the 134 novelty detection scores and taxonomic classification probabilities for four taxonomic 135 ranks (class, order, family, and genus) as output by BERTPhylo (Fig. 1b, see Materials 136 and Methods for details). If the sequence has a higher novelty detection score at any 137 rank, it is classified as an out-of-distribution (OOD) sequence; otherwise, it is an in138 distribution (ID) sequence. For OOD sequences (see example in Fig. 2i), subtrees are 139 determined based on the maximum classification probability at the lowest rank among 140 the ranks with a lower novelty detection score. Here, sequences receive a low novelty 141 detection score at the order rank but a high score at the family rank, indicating that 142 this sequence likely belongs to the known order (Fabales) while being classified into 143 unknown families within the original tree. For ID sequences, the subtree corresponding 144 to the genus with the highest probability is updated directly (Fig. 2ii). Compared to 145 the standard pipelines, our approach significantly reduces sequence number and length 146 for subsequent alignment and tree inference analyses, thereby increasing the efficiency 147 of managing and updating phylogenetic trees (Fig. 3). Specifically, our method reduces 148 the time complexity from O ( NL log L ) + O ( N 2 ) to O ( nl log l ) + O ( n 2 ) , where N and 149 L represent the total number and maximum length of sequences in the original tree, 150 while n and l denote the total number and maximum length of sequences in the subtree 151 requiring update. For instance, when the updated sequence belongs to an unknown 152 taxon of the order Malpighiales in the original tree, the time to align and update this 153 subtree is only 4 minutes, which accounts for merely 0 . 33% of the time required by 154 the standard pipelines. 155

# 2.2 Augmenting traditional approaches with BERTPhylo to locate the taxonomic units of new sequences
BERTPhylo identifies the taxonomic unit of a new sequence in the original tree 158 through two essential tasks: novelty detection and taxonomic classification. Therefore, 159 we evaluated the performance of BERTPhylo on these two tasks separately. 160

Novelty detection. Given a phylogenetic tree (here referring to the tree under 161 Embryophyta), a new sequence may belong to an unknown taxon at the genus rank 162 but to a known taxon at the higher rank. Therefore, to determine the taxonomic unit 163 of a new sequence, we need to identify the lowest rank where the sequence is classi164 fied as a known (i.e. ID) taxon. Notably, BERTPhylo is the first method to achieve 165 this task by generating a novelty detection score for each rank. In a well-performing 166 novelty detection model, OOD sequences receive higher scores, while ID sequences 167 receive lower scores. 168

To evaluate the effectiveness of these scores, we calculate the area under the 169 receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the area under the precision170 recall curve (AUPR) metrics (Fig. 4a). Additionally, we fine-tune DNABERT [34] with 171 randomly initialized hierarchical linear probes (HLPs) on the PlantSeqs training set to 172 assess the effectiveness of our training strategy. We observe that BERTPhylo exhibits 173 good detection performance at all taxonomic ranks, with an AUROC of 98 . 27% at 174 the class level. Compared to DNABERT, the maximum improvement exceeds 36 . 5% , 175 demonstrating that feature selection from the first 10 layers and two-step fine-tuning 176 strategy outperform the commonly used fine-tuning approach. From the density distri177 bution of novelty detection scores, BERTPhylo generates more distinguishable scores 178 for ID and OOD sequences, respectively, with most ID sequences obtaining lower 179 scores and OOD sequences obtaining relatively higher scores (Fig. 4b). 180

Taxonomic classification. Identifying the taxon is one of the oldest and most 181 frequent challenges in systematic biology. Traditional methods either find the most 182 similar sequences in reference databases (BLAST [46] and MMSeqs2 [47]) or pre183 dict the taxonomic origin of k-mers queries (Kraken2 [48]), while deep learning-based 184 methods learn patterns and features from large-scale sequence data to achieve efficient 185 classification and identification (BERTax [49]). For a meaningful comparison, tradi186

tional methods use the training set of PlantSeqs as reference database, while deep 187

learning-based methods leverage their respective open source pre-trained models to 188 fine-tune randomly initialized hierarchical linear probes (HLPs) on the same dataset. 189 We used precision, recall and F1-score, the most important and commonly used 190 metrics for taxonomic classification [50], to calculate the performance of benchmark 191 methods across four taxonomic ranks. Precision and recall gauge classifier prediction 192 accuracy and its ability to identify positive taxa, respectively, while F1-score repre193 sents their harmonic mean. To avoid metric bias stemming from data imbalance, we 194 adopt a macro-average approach for each metric, ensuring equal weight across cat195 egories (Table 1). Compared with deep learning-based methods, BERTPhylo shows 196 clear advantages across all metrics and ranks, with a maximum improvement of 9 . 48% 197 (in macro-F1 at the family rank) and an average improvement of 5 . 54% . However, 198 traditional methods outperformed all deep learning-based methods, possibly because 199 the complex sequences that artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms excel in handling, 200 such as those involving long-range sequence homology, are less likely to be present in 201 the test set [49, 51]. This analysis is further corroborated by combining MMseqs2 with 202 BERTPhylo, leading to additional enhancements across almost all metrics, notably 203 a 5 . 04% increase in macro-F1 at the class rank. The results using micro-average and 204 weighted average are consistent with the results of macro-average (Supplementary 205 Tables S1 and S2). In Supplementary Figure S1, we also show the confusion matri206 ces of BERTPhylo at the four taxonomic ranks, which provide a detailed view of the 207 model predictions for all taxa at each taxonomic rank. 208 To better assess performance across all abundance thresholds, we further presented 209 a comparative analysis of the macro-average Precision-Recall (PR) and Receiver 210 Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves for deep learning-based methods (Fig. 5a,b, 211 Supplementary Figures S2 and S3). The PR curves offer insights into the classifiers' 212 prediction accuracy and class coverage, whereas the ROC curves assess sensitivity 213 and specificity across classes. BERTPhylo demonstrates a marked improvement over 214 DNABERT and BERTax. Additionally, we delineate the PR and ROC curves for these 215 methods across various categories (Fig. 5c,d, Supplementary Figures S4 and S5). All 216 methods employ weighted cross-entropy loss to address category imbalance during 217 training; however, BERTPhylo's strategy of initial linear probing followed by fine218 tuning of the entire model significantly enhances its capability to capture distinctive 219 class features. Notably, in the class rank AUROC, BERTPhylo shows a substantial 220 reduction in the performance disparity observed over DNABERT and BERTax, with 221 differences in AUROC shrinking from 10 . 87% and 30 . 51% down to as low as 0 . 94% . 222 This trend is consistent across all ranks in both ROC and PR curves. Despite these 223 advances, challenges persist, particularly at taxonomic ranks like family and order, 224 where category size and sample imbalance are more pronounced. For instance, the 225 average precision (AveP) for Rubiaceae at the family rank and Cucurbitales at the 226 order rank are only 57 . 58% and 53 . 98% , respectively. Hence, addressing class imbal227 ance and the few-shot problem in DNA sequence data remains a critical frontier for 228 enhancement through AI-driven methods. 229

# 2.3 Resolution of phylogenetic trees constructed with 230 high-attention regions 231
To investigate whether the high-attention regions provided by BERTPhylo encap232 sulate sufficient informative sites to substitute full-length sequences in phylogenetic 233 tree construction, we conducted a comparative analysis of phylogenetic trees con234 structed using high-attention and low-attention regions of sequences, respectively. We 235 divided each sequence equally into three regions and sorted these regions based on 236 the attention weights generated by the last transformer block of the BERT module 237 in BERTPhylo to pick high- and low-attention regions (see Materials and Methods 238 for details). We validated our approach using the dataset of 20 orders as depicted in 239 Figure 2. Only orders encompassing a minimum of two genera were retained, culmi240 nating in the selection of 11 orders for subsequent analyses. By taking the angiosperm 241 order Rosales as an example, the results indicate that high-attention regions facilitate 242 a superior resolution of the phylogenetic topology, while in the topography constructed 243 using low-attention regions, species from the genera Ficus and Artocarpus were inter244 spersed (Fig. 6). Similar scenarios were observed in other six orders of angiosperms 245 (i.e. Asparagales, Fabales, Gentianales, Lamiales, Malpighiales, and Poales). In the 246 remaining four orders, comparable phylogenetic topologies were attained using both 247 datasets (Supplementary Figure S6). Our findings suggest that the high-attention 248 regions extracted by BERTPhylo are enriched with genetic information pertinent to 249 resolve the phylogenetic relationships among species. 250

# 2.4 Differential performance of various markers in taxonomic 251 classification and novelty detection 252
To further evaluate the effect of the model on different molecular markers, we analyzed 253 the performance of nine molecular markers within the PlantSeqs dataset in terms of 254 novelty detection and taxonomic classification. Among these nine markers, six are 255 from the chloroplast genome, including both coding genes ( atp B, mat K, rbc L) and 256 intergenic spacer regions ( rpl 32trn L, trn Ltrn F, trn Hpsb A), while three others (5S 257 rRNA, 28S rRNA, ITS) are from the nuclear genome. It is important to note that 258 during the BERTPhylo model training, all sequences are treated equitably, without 259 bias towards any specific molecular marker. Our findings indicate that performance 260 varies across different markers and performance for the same marker also varies across 261 tasks. For example, the two nulcear markers (28S rRNA, ITS) as well as one IGS 262 region from the chlroplast genome ( trn Ltrn F) demonstrate superior performance in 263 novelty detection tasks, while other plastid markers ( rpl 32trn L, trn Hpsb A, and rbc L) 264 perform relatively poorly (Fig. 7a). For taxonomic classification, trn Ltrn F and rbc L 265 excel in all assessed metrics, whereas atp B and trn Hpsb A show comparatively weaker 266 performance (Fig. 7b,c,d). 267

- 312 application in phylogenetic inference is still in its infancy. The continual growth in the 313

# 4 Materials and Methods 344

# 4.1 Description of the BERTPhylo method 345
BERTPhylo enhances the efficiency of phylogenetic inference by reducing the input for 346 alignment and tree inference tools. This is accomplished by pinpointing the taxonomic 347 unit of a new sequence and extracting potentially valuable regions for the subtree 348 sequences (Fig. 1a). Drawing inspiration from the taxonomy we use should reflect 349 shared ancestry (i.e. phylogeny) [54-56], we infer the taxonomic unit of a sequence 350 based on its taxonomic hierarchy. Furthermore, given that transformer attention can 351 capture biological signals [34, 35], we use attention scores to identify potentially valu352 able regions in sequences. Subsequently, tree inference tools update the topology of 353 the subtree, allowing for more targeted and efficient utilization of these tools. 354

- Tokenization . Given the widespread application of 3-mers in computational genomics 461

# Abstract
Understanding the phylogenetic relationships among species is crucial for com19 prehending major evolutionary transitions, serving as the foundation for many 20 biological studies. Despite the ever-growing volume of sequence data providing a 21 significant opportunity for biological research, constructing reliable phylogenetic 22 trees effectively becomes more challenging for current analytical methods. In this 23 study, we introduce a novel solution to accelerate phylogeny inference using a 24 pretrained DNA language model. Our approach identifies the taxonomic unit of 25 a newly collected sequence using existing taxonomic classification systems and 26 updates the corresponding subtree, akin to surgical corrections on a given phy27 logenetic tree. Specifically, we leverage a pretrained BERT network to obtain 28 high-dimensional sequence representations, which are used not only to deter29 mine the subtree to be updated but also identify potentially valuable regions for 30 subtree construction. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, named 31

3

BERTPhylo, through experiments on our established PlantSeqs dataset, focusing 32 on Embryophyta. Our findings provide the first evidence that phylogenetic trees 33 can be constructed by automatically selecting the most informative regions of 34 sequences, without manual selection of molecular markers. This discovery offers 35 a robust guide for further research into the functional aspects of different regions 36 of DNA sequences, enriching our understanding of biology. 37

# 1 Introduction 40
- Phylogenetic trees serve as fundamental pillars in biological research, elucidating evo41 lutionary relationships among organisms and offering profound insights into their 42 shared history [1-3]. In addition, they play a pivotal role, for instance, in pinpoint43 ing distinct species communities to refine conservation strategies [4-6], in deciphering 44 virus origins [7-9], or even in elucidating cancer progression and guiding therapies [1045 13]. For nearly two decades, molecular phylogenies have primarily relied on data from 46 a few genes obtained through PCR amplification and Sanger sequencing. However, 47 advancements in sequencing technologies have resulted in large-scale datasets contain48 ing orders of magnitude more genes, posing challenges to accurately reconstructing the 49 tree of life [14, 15]. On the one hand, the exponential growth in the quantity of genetic 50 data intensifies computational and storage burdens, leading to substantial time con51 straints and a super-exponential rise in the demand for computational and storage 52 resources. On the other hand, the longer sequences (up to entire genomes) may not 53 only challenge the ability of computational resources but also contain inconsistencies 54 or noise, leading to misleading or less precise results [16, 17]. 55 Traditional phylogenetic tree construction methods are typically divided into two 56 categories: distance-based and character-based. In the context of species tree infer57 ence, distance methods involve calculating genetic distances between species pairs 58 and using resulting matrices to build trees. Character-based methods compare all 59 DNA sequences in an alignment simultaneously, considering one site at a time to cal60 culate scores for each tree. These methods include maximum parsimony, maximum 61 likelihood, and Bayesian inference [18]. However, identifying the tree with the highest 62 score requires comparing all possible trees, which is computationally infeasible due to 63 the NP-hard nature of tree construction [19, 20]. To mitigate computational burdens, 64 various heuristic tree search methods focusing on accelerating and parallelizing cal65 culations have been developed, such as DupTree [21], FastTree [22], PhyloBayes MPI 66 [23], ExaBayes [24], and RAxML-NG [25]. These heuristic tree search methods are 67 not guaranteed to find the best tree, but make it feasible to analyse large data sets 68 [18]. Nonetheless, there is considerable room for improving computational efficiency 69 while maintaining accuracy, making the balance between the two a challenging and 70 pressing issue. 71

Recent advances in deep learning offer promising opportunities for phylogenetic 72 inference, which can be broadly categorized into classification-based and distance73 based methods. Classification-based methods treat phylogenetic inference as a classi74 fication problem, aiming to train neural networks to predict the topology of sequences 75 [26, 27]. Distance-based methods utilize neural networks to improve distance repre76 sentation, addressing challenges such as phylogenetic placement problems and data 77 imputation problems in incomplete distance matrices [28-30]. However, applying deep 78 learning to phylogenetic inference is still in its infancy [31]. Classification-based meth79 ods struggle with scalability and cannot infer branch lengths. Moreover, training deep 80 learning models requires large datasets, but benchmark data with known 'true' phy81 logenies are rare. As a result, almost all studies use simulated data for training, which 82 may not accurately reflect the complexity and diversity of real biological systems, lim83 iting the generalization performance of models on empirical data [32]. Additionally, 84 existing applications are predominantly based on convolutional neural network (CNN) 85 structures, which may not always outperform traditional tree construction methods 86 [33]. As large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language under87 standing, their application to genome modeling problems has also increased [34-38]. 88 Due to the similarities between DNA sequences and natural languages, genomic LLMs 89 built on the Transformer architecture [39] with self-attention mechanism can skillfully 90 model genomic information by capturing long-range dependencies. Such models have 91 recently achieved unprecedented success across various downstream tasks, as exem92 plified by the generation of DNA sequences [36], or the prediction of promoters [34], 93 enhancers [40], and chromatin profiles [38]. Despite these advances, gaps remain in 94 applying LLMs to phylogenetic inference. 95

Amid these challenges, we here introduce a novel program called BERTPhylo, 96 designed to accelerate phylogenetic inference by using a pretrained DNA language 97 model [34], which is constructed and trained following the Bidirectional Encoder 98 Representations from Transformers (BERT) [41] to capture global and transferrable 99 understanding of DNA sequences based on up and downstream nucleotide contexts. 100 As depicted in Figure 1a, BERTPhylo built upon existing taxonomic classification 101 systems to identify the taxonomic unit of a given sequence without performing any 102 operations on it. The network's attention weight on the sequence can also identify 103 potentially valuable genetic regions (hereafter referred to as high-attention regions) 104 that contain adequate informative sites for robust phylogenetic tree construction. We, 105 therefore, propose a novel pipeline based on BERTPhylo, which constructs subtrees 106 for the clades of the new sequences' taxonomic units using only high-attention regions, 107 instead of constructing a complete phylogenetic tree using full-length sequences. In 108 contrast to standard pipelines that align and analyze all sequences simultaneously (e.g. 109 BuddySuite [42], ETE3 [43], and MEGA [44]), our pipeline reduces the number and 110 length of input sequences for subsequent alignment and tree analyses, thereby signif111 icantly decreasing the tree construction time. Importantly, BERTPhylo achieves this 112 speedup without compromising topology accuracy by integrating deep learning with 113 traditional tree construction tools. To validate this innovative approach, we created 114 a dataset called PlantSeqs, which contains 157 , 742 DNA sequences of Embryophyta. 115

These sequences were downloaded from the National Center for Biotechnology Infor116 mation (NCBI) and covered nine commonly used molecular markers (see Materials 117 and Methods for details). In addition to evaluating the effectiveness of the model, we 118 cross-referenced the results with previous studies, demonstrating the efficiency and 119 precision of BERTPhylo. 120

To illustrate the process of updating a phylogenetic tree using BERTPhylo results, 124 Figure 2 presents a simplified example. The original tree comprises 677 species of 125 20 orders from Embryophyta. The sequences of these species were selected from the 126 PlantSeqs dataset. We concatenated all molecular markers of each species for tree 127 construction, with the total lengths ranging from 2 , 493 bp to 7 , 705 bp. For instance, when the updated sequence belongs to an unknown 152 taxon of the order Malpighiales in the original tree, the time to align and update this 153 subtree is only 4 minutes, which accounts for merely 0 . 33% of the time required by 154 the standard pipelines. 155

# 2.2 Augmenting traditional approaches with BERTPhylo to locate the taxonomic units of new sequences
BERTPhylo identifies the taxonomic unit of a new sequence in the original tree 158 through two essential tasks: novelty detection and taxonomic classification. Therefore, 159 we evaluated the performance of BERTPhylo on these two tasks separately. 160

Novelty detection. Given a phylogenetic tree (here referring to the tree under 161 Embryophyta), a new sequence may belong to an unknown taxon at the genus rank 162 but to a known taxon at the higher rank. Therefore, to determine the taxonomic unit 163 of a new sequence, we need to identify the lowest rank where the sequence is classi164 fied as a known (i.e. ID) taxon. Notably, BERTPhylo is the first method to achieve 165 this task by generating a novelty detection score for each rank. In a well-performing 166 novelty detection model, OOD sequences receive higher scores, while ID sequences 167 receive lower scores. 168

To evaluate the effectiveness of these scores, we calculate the area under the 169 receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the area under the precision170 recall curve (AUPR) metrics (Fig. 4a). Additionally, we fine-tune DNABERT [34] with 171 randomly initialized hierarchical linear probes (HLPs) on the PlantSeqs training set to 172 assess the effectiveness of our training strategy. We observe that BERTPhylo exhibits 173 good detection performance at all taxonomic ranks, with an AUROC of 98 . 27% at 174 the class level. Compared to DNABERT, the maximum improvement exceeds 36 . 5% , 175 demonstrating that feature selection from the first 10 layers and two-step fine-tuning 176 strategy outperform the commonly used fine-tuning approach. From the density distri177 bution of novelty detection scores, BERTPhylo generates more distinguishable scores 178 for ID and OOD sequences, respectively, with most ID sequences obtaining lower 179 scores and OOD sequences obtaining relatively higher scores (Fig. 4b). 180

Taxonomic classification. Identifying the taxon is one of the oldest and most 181 frequent challenges in systematic biology. Traditional methods either find the most 182 similar sequences in reference databases (BLAST [46] and MMSeqs2 [47]) or pre183 dict the taxonomic origin of k-mers queries (Kraken2 [48]), while deep learning-based 184 methods learn patterns and features from large-scale sequence data to achieve efficient 185 classification and identification (BERTax [49]). For a meaningful comparison, tradi186

tional methods use the training set of PlantSeqs as reference database, while deep 187

learning-based methods leverage their respective open source pre-trained models to 188 fine-tune randomly initialized hierarchical linear probes (HLPs) on the same dataset. 189 We used precision, recall and F1-score, the most important and commonly used 190 metrics for taxonomic classification [50], to calculate the performance of benchmark 191 methods across four taxonomic ranks. Precision and recall gauge classifier prediction 192 accuracy and its ability to identify positive taxa, respectively, while F1-score repre193 sents their harmonic mean. To avoid metric bias stemming from data imbalance, we 194 adopt a macro-average approach for each metric, ensuring equal weight across cat195 egories (Table 1). Compared with deep learning-based methods, BERTPhylo shows 196 clear advantages across all metrics and ranks, with a maximum improvement of 9 . 48% 197 (in macro-F1 at the family rank) and an average improvement of 5 . 54% . However, 198 traditional methods outperformed all deep learning-based methods, possibly because 199 the complex sequences that artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms excel in handling, 200 such as those involving long-range sequence homology, are less likely to be present in 201 the test set [49, 51]. This analysis is further corroborated by combining MMseqs2 with 202 BERTPhylo, leading to additional enhancements across almost all metrics, notably 203 a 5 . 04% increase in macro-F1 at the class rank. The results using micro-average and 204 weighted average are consistent with the results of macro-average (Supplementary 205 Tables S1 and S2). BERTPhylo demonstrates a marked improvement over 214 DNABERT and BERTax. To investigate whether the high-attention regions provided by BERTPhylo encap232 sulate sufficient informative sites to substitute full-length sequences in phylogenetic 233 tree construction, we conducted a comparative analysis of phylogenetic trees con234 structed using high-attention and low-attention regions of sequences, respectively. Training protocol and objective . BERTPhylo utilizes the first 10 layer weights of DNABERT to initialize the BERT module, while the HLPs are initialized randomly. Instead of typical fine-tuning approaches like full fine-tuning (updating all model parameters) or linear probing (updating only the last linear layer, or "head"), BERTPhylo employs a two-step training strategy (Fig. 1c). In the first step, the BERT

module remains frozen, and only HLPs are trained for a maximum of 100 epochs. Subsequently, all layers are unfrozen, and the entire model is trained for up to 30 additional epochs. Throughout training, learning rate reduction occurs when a plateau is reached, and early stopping based on the validation set is applied. To prevent bias toward predicting the most common taxa, class weights were calculated for each taxonomic rank, balancing the taxa and allowing the model to focus more on samples from underrepresented taxa. The entire model was trained using a weighted cross-entropy loss, defined as follows:

L = 1 N N ∑ s =1 N r ∑ i =1 ∑ r ∈ R -w r,i y ′ r,s,i log exp( y r,s,i ) ∑ s r j =1 exp( y r,s,j ) ,

where

w r,i = 1 N r × ∑ N r j =1 n r,j n r,i .

Here y ′ r,s,i and y r,s,i are the ground-truth and predicted values of taxon i of rank r 473 for sequence s , n r,i is the number of samples for taxon i of rank r , N r is the number 474 of taxa of rank r , R = { class, order, family, genus } , and L is the total loss. 475
